title: Coil-built tall storage canister
subtitle: A lidded canister in air-dry clay with a scored surface texture
excerpt: A tall coil-built canister about 18 cm high sits on a slab base and takes a fitted slab lid with a clay knob. The outer walls are scored with horizontal lines before drying for a textured finish. The entire piece works in air-dry clay: no kiln needed. Once sealed it serves as a decorative storage container.
sourceNotes: Coil-building method derived from first principles. Historical coil construction referenced from Encyclopedia Britannica 11th edition (1911) pottery entry. V&A open-access collection for comparative coil-built vessel form reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rope of clay rolled between the palms and the work surface to an even diameter, stacked in rings to build vessel walls
The joining method: roughen both surfaces with a needle, apply clay slip, then press together
The drying stage where clay holds its shape firmly but remains damp enough to blend, trim, and score
Fully air-dried and unfired; fragile, ready for surface sealing
A flat sheet of clay rolled to an even thickness, used here as the base and lid of the canister

content.text: A tall lidded canister about 18 cm high and 10 cm in diameter holds dry goods on a kitchen shelf or acts as a desk storage jar. The walls are built from stacked
coils

of air-dry clay blended together on the interior to form a continuous wall; the exterior is left with scored horizontal lines for texture. No kiln is needed. Once sealed, the canister works as a display container: store dry items only, as air-dry clay is not watertight.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay body thinned with water)
PVA glue diluted 50/50 with water (for sealing)

content.text: Preparation

Coil-building a tall form takes two or three sessions as lower coils need to firm a little before supporting more weight above. Plan to build the bottom third, leave it for one to two hours covered loosely, then continue. Prepare a pot of clay slip before beginning. Work on a canvas sheet and keep rolled coils covered with a damp cloth while not in use.
Making the base slab
Roll a
slab
to 8 mm thick. Cut a circle 12 cm in diameter using a template and a fettling knife.
Smooth the edges of the base circle with a damp sponge. Set it aside on the canvas and allow it to stiffen for 20 minutes before attaching the first coil ring.
Building the walls
Roll coils to 15 mm diameter between your palms and the canvas. Keep them even along their length. Roll enough for three or four rings before starting to build.

Score the top perimeter of the base slab and the underside of the first coil with a needle tool. Apply slip to both faces. Lay the coil around the perimeter of the base circle and press down firmly, joining the ends of the coil by scoring and slipping the join line. Use the
score-and-slip
method for every subsequent coil ring as well.

Blend the interior of each coil join with a wooden rib, pressing clay downward from the top coil into the one below. Work around the full interior circumference before adding the next coil. The interior wall should be smooth and continuous with no visible coil gaps.
Leave the exterior coil ridges unblended for the first six rings. These ridges will form the scored texture in the finishing stage.

After six rings (roughly the bottom third of the canister), cover loosely with a cloth and allow the walls to firm for one to two hours. The lower walls need to support the weight of further coils without bulging outward.
Continue adding coils in the same way until the wall reaches 17 cm above the base. The wall thickness should stay at 8 mm throughout: check it by pinching the wall between your thumb and forefinger.
At the rim, the final coil should be blended smooth on both interior and exterior to create a clean, even top edge for the lid to rest on.
Scoring the surface texture
Once the walls have reached a firm
leather-hard

state, score horizontal lines across the exterior coil ridges with a needle tool. Hold the needle tool at a shallow angle and draw it around the circumference in a continuous line, following the natural ridge of each coil. The result is a series of evenly spaced horizontal grooves that emphasise the coil structure.
Making the lid

Measure the interior rim diameter of the finished canister with calipers or a ruler. Cut a slab circle 2 mm less than this diameter so the lid drops in slightly rather than resting flat on top. A lid that rests on the rim rather than dropping in looks neater and is easier to lift.

Roll a small ball of clay into a cylinder 15 mm high and 20 mm in diameter for the lid knob. Flatten the base of the knob, score both the knob base and the lid centre, apply slip, and press firmly. Blend the join with a rib.
Leave the lid to dry separately from the canister body. They must dry independently: drying them in contact causes the rim to crack as both pieces shrink.
Drying
Allow both the canister body and the lid to air-dry to
bone-dry

over three to five days at room temperature. Cover loosely with a cloth for the first 24 hours to slow surface drying. A tall vessel dries unevenly: the rim dries faster than the base. Rotating the canister 180 degrees on its base each day helps even out the drying rate.
Sealing and finishing

Apply two coats of 50/50 PVA and water to all surfaces of both the canister and the lid. Use a brush to work the sealer into the scored grooves. Allow each coat to dry fully before the next. For a decorative finish, paint the scored grooves with a contrasting acrylic colour before sealing, wiping the raised ridges clean to leave the colour in the recessed lines only.
Use and care

This canister is decorative. Air-dry clay is not waterproof and is not food-safe without a tested glaze. Use it to store dry, non-food items: art supplies, small stationery, dried botanicals. Do not wash by immersion. Wipe the exterior with a dry cloth. The scored surface will hold dust: brush it out with a soft brush monthly.
Variations
Make a set of three canisters at different heights: 10 cm, 14 cm, and 18 cm, with graduated diameters of 8, 10, and 12 cm, to form a matching kitchen or desk display set.
Skip the horizontal scoring. Leave the coil ridges as they are on the outside. This gives a rougher, more rustic look.
Press a sprig mould motif onto the exterior wall at leather-hard before scoring, centred between two scored lines, for a formal decorated surface.
Troubleshooter

items.cause: Coils were added too fast before the lower walls were firm enough to support the weight
items.fix: Allow lower walls to firm for one to two hours between building sessions. If a bulge develops, gently press it back while the clay is still leather-hard

items.problem: Coil join lines visible on the interior wall
items.cause: The interior was not blended thoroughly after each ring was added
items.fix: Blend the interior immediately after each coil is placed. Use a wooden rib to press clay from the upper coil downward into the lower one, working all the way around

items.cause: The rim is the thinnest, most exposed part and dries fastest, creating tension
items.fix: Cover the rim with a strip of damp cloth while the body catches up in drying speed. Check every six hours and re-dampen if needed

items.problem: Lid does not fit: too loose or too tight
items.cause: The lid diameter was measured before the clay had fully shrunk, or was cut to the exterior rim diameter rather than the interior
items.fix: Measure the interior rim when the canister is at leather-hard, then cut the lid. Air-dry clay shrinks 5-8% as it dries: account for this by cutting the lid 2-3 mm smaller than the measured interior

items.problem: Base cracks away from the first coil ring
items.cause: The base and the coil dried at different rates, or the score-and-slip join was not complete
items.fix: At leather-hard, press fresh slip into the crack, fill with a thin clay coil, and smooth. Allow to dry slowly with a cloth cover
